intro: Six things to try. None of them is a test question; they are the ideas behind the questions, made so you can push on them.

items.title: Which level?
items.blurb: Real responsibilities, one at a time. Sort them into federal, state or local council. Sixty seconds, or take your time.
items: Issuing Australian passports
Passports, like borders and citizenship, are national matters.
Running the Australian Defence Force
Defence is a federal responsibility under the Constitution.
Deciding who can migrate to Australia
Immigration and visas are federal.
Printing banknotes and minting coins
Currency is federal; one dollar works in every state.
Collecting income tax
The Australian Taxation Office is a federal agency.
Paying the age pension
Pensions and other Centrelink payments are federal.
Medicare rebates for a doctor's visit
Medicare is a federal scheme.
Running embassies overseas
Foreign affairs is federal; the states do not have embassies.
Checking goods at the border for customs
Customs and Border Force are federal.
Setting the rules for marriage
Marriage law is a federal power listed in the Constitution.
Delivering the mail through Australia Post
Postal services are federal.
Licensing radio and television broadcasters
Communications are a federal responsibility.
Running government primary and secondary schools
State governments run public schools and employ their teachers.
Victoria Police
Each state and territory has its own police force.
Trains, trams and buses in Melbourne
Public transport is run or contracted by the state government.
Issuing driver licences
Licences and car registration are state matters.
Building and maintaining freeways
Major roads are state responsibilities; councils handle local streets.
Fire and emergency services
Fire brigades, the SES and ambulances are organised by the states.
Running prisons
Prisons and most criminal law are state responsibilities.
TAFE colleges
Vocational training is mostly run by the states.
Electricity and water supply rules
Utilities are regulated at state level.
Deciding school term dates
Each state sets its own term dates.
Setting the speed limit on a highway
Road rules and highway limits are state matters.
Fishing licences
Recreational fishing is regulated by the state.
Mowing and maintaining the local park
Parks, playgrounds and sports ovals are council work.
Fixing a cracked footpath
Footpaths and local streets belong to the council.
Registering your dog or cat
Pet registration is a council service.
Running the public library
Local libraries are funded and run by councils.
Approving a permit to build a house extension
Planning and building permits for homes go through the council.
Parking rules on local streets
Councils set and enforce local parking.
Street lighting in your street
Councils arrange lighting on local roads.
Inspecting a cafe's kitchen for food safety
Councils carry out food-safety inspections of local businesses.
Running the community swimming pool
Leisure centres and pools are usually council facilities.
Organising the local festival
Community events are a council role.
Maternal and child health nurse visits for new babies
In Victoria, councils run the maternal and child health service.
Deciding where a new kindergarten goes
Councils plan and often run local kindergartens.

items.title: Which branch?
items.blurb: Something happens in government. Is it the legislature, the executive or the judiciary at work?
items: The House of Representatives debates a bill
Parliament, both houses, is the legislature: it makes and changes laws.
The Senate votes to pass a bill
Voting on bills is law-making, the legislature's job.
A parliamentary committee reviews a proposed law
Committees are part of Parliament's work on laws.
Parliament repeals a law from the 1950s
Only the legislature can make or unmake a law.
MPs vote on the budget
The budget is passed as bills through Parliament.
A new law receives royal assent
Royal assent is the final step of the legislative process.
Parliament changes the voting age
Changing a law is the legislature's role.
The Passport Office processes an application
Government departments carry out laws: the executive.
A minister announces funding for a new program
Ministers lead the executive and direct departments.
Centrelink pays a student allowance
Departments put laws into action by delivering services.
The Australian Federal Police investigate a fraud
Police enforce the law; they are part of the executive.
Cabinet decides government policy on energy
Cabinet is the senior ministers, the heart of the executive.
The Prime Minister appoints a new minister
The Prime Minister leads the executive government.
The Tax Office sends out a tax bill
Collecting tax under the law is executive work.
Border Force searches a container at the port
Enforcing customs law is executive work.
A magistrate decides whether a driver broke the law
Courts apply the law to cases: the judiciary.
The High Court rules that a law goes against the Constitution
Interpreting the Constitution is the High Court's job.
A judge sentences an offender to community service
Sentencing happens in court, in the judiciary.
A court decides what a word in a law means
Interpreting laws is the judiciary's role.
A jury finds the accused not guilty
Juries are part of the court process.
A court settles a dispute between two businesses
Resolving disputes under the law is judicial work.
An appeal court overturns an earlier decision
Appeals are heard by higher courts in the judiciary.
A judge orders the release of a person wrongly held
Courts check that the executive acts within the law.

items.title: Which principle?
items.blurb: Something happens in the justice system. Which principle is at work: fairness, equality or access?
items: Both sides get to present their evidence
Fairness means impartial processes where each side can be heard.
A judge steps aside because the accused is a neighbour
Removing a possible bias protects fairness.
The accused is shown the evidence against them before the trial
You cannot answer a case you have not seen: fairness.
A jury is chosen at random from the community
A random jury guards against bias, which is fairness.
A decision-maker ignores who the people are and looks only at the evidence
Impartiality is the core of fairness.
A witness is given time to answer and is not shouted down
A fair hearing means each person can put their case.
A footballer and a shop assistant get the same fine for the same offence
Equality: the law applies the same way whatever your status.
A minister is charged like anyone else after breaking the law
Nobody is above the law: equality.
The same speed limit applies to every driver on the road
Laws apply to everyone in the same way.
Two people who commit the same crime in the same circumstances get the same penalty
Treating like cases alike is equality before the law.
A court refuses to give a celebrity a quieter, private hearing
Equality means no special treatment because of fame.
A free duty lawyer helps someone who cannot afford one
Access: people can understand and use the legal system.
Court forms are rewritten in plain English
Making the system understandable improves access.
A regional court holds hearings by video link
Reducing distance barriers improves access.
Legal aid covers the costs of a person on a low income
Cost is a barrier to justice; legal aid lowers it.
Information about court processes is published in ten community languages
Language is a barrier; translation improves access.
A court building is made wheelchair accessible
Physical access to the court is part of access to justice.
Court opens on Saturday mornings for people who work all week
Opening hours that suit people improve access.

items.title: The double majority
items.blurb: Move the Yes vote in each state and watch a referendum pass or fail. Then try the 1977 trap: a national Yes that still failed.

items.title: Form a government
items.blurb: Deal out 150 seats and see who can govern. Majority, minority, coalition or hung parliament, with the 76 line drawn.

items.title: Fix this law
items.blurb: A council wants a law about e-scooters near the beach. Build it clause by clause and check it against the five characteristics of an effective law.
items.intro: A council wants to stop dangerous e-scooter riding on the beach path. Choose one clause from each row. The law assembles itself at the top, and the five checks update as you go.

options.why: Dangerously is a judgement. Riders and officers will disagree about what it means.

options.t: ride an e-scooter faster than 10 km/h
options.why: A number can be measured and understood by everyone.

options.t: ride an e-scooter in a way that annoys people
options.why: What annoys one person does not annoy another. Not clear, not enforceable.
How near is near? A boundary nobody can see cannot be followed.

options.t: on the shared path between the pier and the surf club
options.why: A named stretch with two landmarks. Anyone can tell if they are on it.
Clear, but it bans scooters everywhere, which goes far beyond the problem and most residents would not support it.
Busy is not a time. Riders cannot plan around it.

options.t: between 10 am and 6 pm from December to February
options.why: Exact hours and months are easy to know and to check.
Clear, but a year-round ban when the path is empty in winter is more than the community asked for.

columns.label: What happens if you break it

options.why: A law with no consequence cannot be enforced.

options.t: a $100 fine issued by a council officer
options.why: A set consequence and a named enforcer make the law enforceable.

options.t: the rider may be banned from the beach for life
options.why: Enforceable, but a lifetime ban for a speeding scooter does not match what the community thinks is fair.

options.t: it is filed at the council office
options.why: A law nobody sees cannot be followed. It must be communicated.

options.t: signs at every path entrance and a notice on the council website
options.why: Signs where the law applies, plus a public notice, make it known.

options.t: it is mentioned once in a council newsletter
options.why: One mention most people will miss is not enough for a law to be known.

options.t: whenever a councillor wants to change it
options.why: A rule that shifts without warning cannot be relied on.

options.t: reviewed every two years after a public survey
options.why: Regular, predictable review keeps the law stable but still able to change, and asking residents keeps it in step with their values.
Stable, but a law that can never respond to change will eventually stop reflecting society's values.
